The soldiers divided his garments by lot and sat down to watch, and over his head the official charge was posted for every passerby to read in the public record of Rome: Jesus, the King of the Jews. The Roman indictment is the Gospel's thesis; Pilate had meant it as the crime, and it stands in Matthew's telling as the truth, nailed up where the world could read it. The mockery at the cross gathered every voice of the week into one chorus. Passersby: “You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save Yourself! If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” The chief priests, scribes, and elders, theological to the end: “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself. He is the King of Israel! Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him. He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him”. Even the robbers crucified beside him “berated Him” in the same words. Every taunt aimed at the same exchange: come down, save yourself, and we will believe. The whole Gospel answers that the refusal to come down is the salvation: he cannot save himself, because he is busy saving others, and the mockers state the condition of the world's faith precisely backwards. He stayed.

From the sixth hour to the ninth, noon to three, “darkness came over all the land”, a darkness Matthew records without explanation, creation itself dimming at midday. “About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, ‘Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?’ which means, ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’” It is the only word from the cross Matthew records, and it is Psalm 22's opening line, the cry of the righteous sufferer, spoken in Aramaic so that the bystanders' misunderstanding is preserved too: “He is calling Elijah”, they said, and someone ran with sour wine on a reed while the rest watched to see if Elijah would come. Psalm 22 ends in vindication and the worship of the nations; whether Jesus quoted its first line as despair or as a pointer to its ending, the Gospel leaves the cry standing in the dark at full weight. Then: “When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, He yielded up His spirit”. Yielded: the death is rendered in a verb of surrender, not seizure. At that moment the second temple scene of the week answered the first: “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom”, torn downward, from God's side. The earth quaked, rocks split, tombs broke open, and Matthew records, with the plainness of a man aware how it sounds, that after the resurrection many holy people who had died came out of those tombs and appeared to many in Jerusalem; the death was already cracking graves before the third day. The verdict of the crucifixion, in Matthew's account, is given not by the council or the crowd or the governor but by the execution squad's commander, standing at the foot of the cross, a Gentile soldier watching a Jewish prisoner die: When the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and all that had happened, they were terrified and said, “Truly this was the Son of God.” And at a distance, where they had been all along, stood the women who had followed from Galilee to serve him, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee's sons, watching. The men had fled; the women stayed; and the first confession of the Son of God over the corpse came from the man who had supervised the killing.

title: He Is Not Here
subtitle: Matthew 27:57–28:20
description: A rich man's tomb, a guard the opposition requested, an empty grave at dawn, and a mountain in Galilee.
paragraphs: The burial was done by a secret disciple with standing. “When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who himself was a disciple of Jesus”. The rich man of chapter 19's warning walked into Pilate's presence and asked for the body of an executed criminal, an act that named his allegiance in the public record at the moment allegiance was most dangerous. Pilate ordered it given. Joseph wrapped the body “in a clean linen cloth, and placed it in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock. Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away”. Isaiah had written that the suffering servant would be assigned a grave with the rich; Matthew simply records a rich man's new tomb receiving him, and two Marys sitting opposite the sepulchre, watching where he was laid. The next day, the Sabbath itself, the chief priests and Pharisees did something remarkable: they went to Pilate with a memory. “Sir”, they said, “we remember that while He was alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’” The enemies remembered the resurrection predictions the disciples kept forgetting. Their request built the resurrection's evidence with their own hands: “give the order that the tomb be secured until the third day. Otherwise, His disciples may come and steal Him away and tell the people He has risen from the dead”. Pilate's answer dismisses them to their own resources: “You have a guard”, Pilate said. “Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how”. So they sealed the stone and posted the watch, Rome's seal and Jerusalem's guard on a dead man's grave: “they went and secured the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard”. No account of the next morning can claim the tomb was unwatched, because the watchmen were the opposition's own idea.

“After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb”. They came to look, not expecting anything but grief, and were met by an earthquake and an angel: “an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, rolled away the stone, and sat on it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothes were white as snow”. The guards, armed men set by professionals to prevent exactly an empty tomb, “trembled in fear of him and became like dead men”, the living watch collapsing while the dead man walked free. The angel's speech to the women is the gospel in miniature, and Matthew lets it stand nearly whole: “Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay”. Then the commission: “Then go quickly and tell His disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead and is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him.’” He is not here: the tomb is commended to their inspection as evidence, the empty place where he lay, and then they are commissioned, the first preachers of the resurrection, and both of them women, in a world that discounted women's testimony in court. Matthew does not argue the point; he just records who got the news first, and who carried it. “So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great joy, and ran to tell His disciples”. Fear and great joy, both at once, at a run.

On the road the risen Jesus met them himself: “Suddenly Jesus met them and said, ‘Greetings!’ They came to Him, grasped His feet, and worshiped Him”. Ordinary greeting, extraordinary feet: they could hold them. This was no ghost and no vision; the same body that was buried had hands and feet they could grasp, and worship is their instant response. His message repeated the angel's, with one word changed that carries the whole restoration in it: “Do not be afraid”, said Jesus. “Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me”. My brothers. The men who had deserted him, denied him, and fled are re-named family by their risen Lord before he has seen them, and Peter, somewhere in the city with his bitter tears, is inside that word. Meanwhile the other report was being prepared. The guards told the chief priests everything, and the council responded the way it had responded all week, with money: “they gave the soldiers a large sum of money and instructed them: ‘You are to say, “His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep”’”. The story refutes itself in the telling, since sleeping witnesses cannot identify thieves, and carried a capital risk for soldiers asleep on watch, which the priests also purchased: “If this report reaches the governor, we will satisfy him”. Matthew adds the epitaph of the cover story: “this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day”. Two reports left that tomb: one carried by women who had seen and held a risen man, one bought by the men who had demanded the grave be sealed. The sealing is what makes the choice between them a choice.

The Gospel closes where the ministry began, in Galilee, on a mountain, with the eleven: “the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted”. Even here, at the summit, worship and doubt stand in the same sentence and the same men, and Matthew, honest to the last verse, does not tidy it. Doubt was no disqualifier; the doubters are inside the group that receives what follows, the most consequential commission ever given: Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you.” All authority, all nations, all that I commanded: the mission that was restricted to the lost sheep of Israel in chapter 10 is now thrown open to the world, on the ground of a cosmic authority claimed without qualification. Baptism in the one name of the three, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching unto obedience, the sermons' demand for doing and not only hearing, extended to the nations. And the book that began with a genealogy, with Emmanuel, God with us, promised in its first chapter, ends on Emmanuel kept: “And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age”. Not I will be, but I am, always, to the end. The genealogy had promised a king descended from Abraham and David. The Gospel delivered a king risen from the dead, reigning over all nations, present with his people to the last day of the age: the record that opened with “the son of David, the son of Abraham” closes with the Son of God sending Abraham's children to gather the world.
